Glossary

    Weaknesses and limits

    Words: 1248

    An honest inventory of what Bash does poorly, and the signals that a task has outgrown it. Without this section, the previous one would just be marketing.

    Key idea #

    Bash has four structural weaknesses that cannot be outsmarted by craft: leaky error handling, no data structures, integer-only arithmetic, and concurrency without synchronization. To these are added two acquired limits: readability degrades sharply past three hundred lines, and portability breaks on two independent axes - different shells and different utilities. None of these make Bash a bad language: they define the territory where it is best. The danger is not the weaknesses, but failing to notice when a task moves outside that territory. The final section lists the warning signs.

    1 · Error handling: set -e is leaky #

    The biggest weakness, and the most dangerous because it looks like a solved problem. set -e creates a false sense of security, but has more holes than any engineer can keep in their head.

    set -euo pipefail

f() { false; echo "will run"; }
if f; then :; fi        # -e disabled

local x=$(false)        # local returns 0
yes | head -n 1         # 141 (SIGPIPE)

    The rule: inside a conditional, to the left of && or ||, inside a function invoked in a conditional, and in local x=$(cmd) - set -e does not trigger. Inversely, enabling pipefail abruptly breaks well-behaved pipelines with head or grep -q when the downstream stage closes the pipe early and the upstream process receives SIGPIPE (exit code 141) from the kernel. Add the absence of exceptions and stack traces, and you have a language where reliable error handling demands personal discipline rather than language guarantees.

    What gets asked: “When does set -e fail to catch an error, and why does pipefail crash on head -n 1?”

    2 · There is no data, only text #

    Bash has only one true data type: strings. Arrays exist, but cannot be passed into functions, nested within each other, or returned outward. Structs do not exist at all.

    # not an array of arrays,
# just a space-separated string
arr=("a b" "c")
other=("${arr[@]}")   # copy like this

f() { local -n ref=$1; }  # bash 4.3+
# no other way to pass an array

cat data.json | jq -r '.items[].id'
# JSON in bash - always via jq

    Any manipulation of JSON, YAML, or CSV requires external tools: jq, yq, awk. For small payloads, that is fine. As soon as you have nested objects, cross-source joins, or schema mutations - you are writing a jq program embedded in a bash program, and nobody will be able to maintain it.

    What gets asked: “How do you pass an array to a function in Bash, and why is it awkward?”

    3 · Integer-only arithmetic #

    Built-in Bash arithmetic does not support floating-point fractions. Period.

    echo $(( 7 / 2 ))        # 3
echo $(( 10 * 95 / 100 )) # 9

echo 'scale=2; 7/2' | bc  # 3.50
awk 'BEGIN{print 7/2}'    # 3.5

    Any percentage, average, or fractional elapsed time requires invoking bc or awk, spawning an external process for every calculation. If a task involves mathematics, Bash is the wrong tool, and no amount of skill changes that.

    What gets asked: “How do you compute an average or percentage in Bash, and why is it cumbersome?”

    4 · Concurrency without synchronization #

    Launching a hundred background jobs is easy. Doing it correctly is not: the language provides no mutexes, queues, or thread-safe shared state.

    for f in *.log; do
  process "$f" &
done
wait            # exit status - not yours

# throttle and capture failures:
printf '%s\0' *.log \
  | xargs -0 -P4 -n1 process

    Two background processes writing to the same file will interleave output lines. A counter incremented inside a subshell remains unchanged outside. And wait without arguments always returns 0 - even if every background job failed; discovering failures requires waiting on each PID individually. While xargs -P and parallel handle trivial cases, anything beyond processing N independent files is your cue to leave Bash.

    What gets asked: “How do you limit parallel jobs in shell, and how do you know if one failed?”

    5 · Readability degrades beyond three hundred lines #

    Bash syntax is optimized for single-line interactive entry, not for reading six months later. Quotes, expansions, and tests combine into text that is hard to scan visually.

    [[ -n "${v:-}" ]] && [[ "${v}" != "x" ]] \
  || { echo "no"; exit 1; }

# condition, action, and error
# handling - in a single line

    As a script grows beyond three hundred lines, fundamental Bash limitations become painful: lack of modules and namespaces, global-by-default variables, and typos that pass unnoticed without set -u. The practical threshold is around three hundred lines: past that, reading the script demands the same esoteric context as writing it, defeating the goal of maintainable engineering.

    What gets asked: “At what boundary should a shell script be rewritten in another language?”

    6 · Portability: two different worlds #

    “Works on my machine” in shell fails for two independent reasons: the wrong shell and the wrong utilities.

    #!/bin/sh
echo ${arr[0]}   # error in dash

sed -i 's/a/b/' f   # GNU
sed -i '' 's/a/b/' f # BSD/macOS

stat -c %s f     # GNU; BSD: -f %z
date -d @0       # GNU; BSD: -r 0

    /bin/sh on Debian and Ubuntu is dash, not Bash: arrays, [[ ]], process substitution, and ${v//a/b} are missing. (local, contrary to popular belief, is supported in dash.) In Alpine containers, the shell is BusyBox ash, and half of standard flags behave differently. On macOS, Bash is stuck at version 3.2, and utilities are BSD.

    The honest, boring solution: either commit to #!/usr/bin/env bash and drop POSIX purity, or check with shellcheck -s sh and renounce convenience. There is no middle ground, and the choice must be made deliberately.

    What gets asked: “How does sh differ from bash, and why do scripts break in Alpine or on macOS?”

    7 · When to move on, and where #

    Signs that Bash is no longer the right tool - any single one is enough:

    • the task requires data structures or JSON beyond a flat list;
    • floating-point arithmetic is needed;
    • real error handling with recovery is necessary;
    • concurrency goes beyond N independent tasks;
    • the script exceeds three hundred lines and continues growing;
    • it will be maintained by engineers unfamiliar with Bash.

    Where to go. Python - when you need data structures and libraries. Go or Rust - when you need a single dependency-free binary on the target host; Go is cheaper in development velocity, Rust in long-term operational reliability, and for replacing a script the former usually decides it. Make - when the problem is about task dependencies rather than linear steps. Ansible or Terraform - when the goal is desired state rather than imperatively executing actions.

    And the inverse rule, equally vital: do not rewrite twenty lines of Bash in Python out of dogma. Maintenance cost scales with size, not language.

    Artifacts: what you have after this page #

    Reading >> Your quantum of life's time · A partnership of dignity with AI · Rewiring your neural network

    The ability to say “Bash does not fit here” and name the reason. Time was well spent if you stopped arguing about languages in the abstract and started citing concrete workload constraints: fractions, nested data, error recovery, script scale. That is the neural rewire - choosing tools stops being a matter of taste and becomes an explicit cost calculation.
